subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Rate of Rise: The Roaster's Curve
description: A micro-lesson that makes Rate of Rise: The Roaster's Curve usable.

hook.text: Professional roasters obsess over 'rate of rise' (RoR)—how quickly the bean temperature increases per minute.

buildup.text: RoR is plotted as a curve on roasting software. The ideal shape looks like a gradually declining slope.

discovery.text: A steadily declining RoR means controlled energy transfer. Spikes or crashes create flavor defects.

twist.text: The same green coffee can taste fruity or ashy, bright or flat, depending entirely on how the RoR curve was managed.

climax.text: Modern roasting is data-driven. Temperature probes, software, and airflow sensors make RoR tracking precise.

punchline.text: A curve on a screen controls thousands of flavor molecules. Data meets craft.

quiz.question: What is 'rate of rise' (RoR) in roasting?
options: How fast the roaster machine heats up
How quickly the bean temperature increases per minute

details.summary: Rate of rise measures how quickly bean temperature increases per minute during roasting. Plotted on a graph, it forms the roasting curve that guides every decision. A steady decline in rate of rise after first crack usually indicates well-controlled development.
details.whyItMatters: Rate of rise is the roaster's primary diagnostic tool. Reading the curve in real time allows precise adjustments that shape acidity, sweetness, and body in the final cup.
takeaways: Rate of rise tracks temperature change per unit of time
A declining rate of rise after first crack signals good control
Sudden spikes or crashes indicate heat application errors

faq.question: What does a flick or spike in the rate of rise curve indicate?
faq.answer: A sudden spike, sometimes called a flick, often means too much heat was applied at once. It can cause scorching or tipping on the bean surface, introducing bitter, charred flavors into the cup.

faq.question: How do roasters use software to track rate of rise?
faq.answer: Roasting software like Cropster or Artisan reads thermocouple data in real time and plots rate of rise alongside bean temperature. Roasters overlay reference profiles to compare batches and maintain consistency.
